newsitem.title: FRANCE: France faces uncertain future after left poll win.
newsitem.headline: France faces uncertain future after left poll win.

text.p: France faced a leap into the unknown on Monday after voters gave the left-wing opposition a stunning victory inconceivable only five weeks ago.
The result of Sunday's parliamentary election runoff set Jacques Chirac's presidency totally on its head.

Triumphantly elected only two years ago this month, Chirac dissolved the National Assembly on April 21 and called a snap election in hopes of ensuring himself a friendly majority for the rest of his seven-year term.
The decision backfired disastrously, opening the floodgates to a voter backlash which will go down in French annals as a misjudgement of monumental proportions.
The president's ruling centre-right coalition lost almost half its 464 lower house seats.

Barring new upsets, Chirac now faces a possible five years as lame-duck president, diminished in the eyes of his people and the world, especially fellow Europeans he not-so-secretly hoped to lead in the emergence of a new political and economic world power.

Chirac is now virtually obliged to appoint Socialist leader Lionel Jospin as prime minister on Monday, inaugurating what could be a period of major uncertainty for France. The constitution bars him from dissolving the chamber again for one year.
Commentators agreed the new situation might be as difficult for Jospin as it would be for Chirac.

"He's only got about two weeks' state of grace," said Serge July, editor of the left-of-centre daily Liberation. "He must act immediately to carry out his campaign promises or he will face the same public rejection as Chirac."

July and others said Jospin's Socialists, unable to claim a parliamentary majority on their own, will have to placate political allies like the Communists or ultra-militant Greens, even before thinking how to "co-habit" in power with Chirac.

With 10 seats left to be declared, the Socialists and their allies had 268 seats, the ecologists seven and the Communists 38 for a total of 313. The Gaullist RPR had 131, the centrist UDF 108, other right-wing candidates 14 and the extreme-right National Front one.
Jospin said the people had voted for a change of direction in European policy, but he did not call into question the planned single European currency.
Jospin has said he supports European economic and monetary union but would not impose a further bout of austerity to meet the strict criteria to qualify France for the single currency in 1999.

Most commentators agreed that unemployment, the number one concern of the French public, was the main reason why so many voters had cast their ballots "against" the government rather than for the opposition.

The Socialists have pledged to create 700,000 jobs for young people, half of them in the public sector, over the next three years, and reduce the working week from 39 hours to 35 over five years without loss of pay.
Chirac glided to victory in May 1995 promising to make the fight against unemployment his prime concern.

In the next two years, however, it rose from 11.5 to 12.8 percent following Chirac's astonishing October 1995 about-face, when he announced that the government's new priority would be to cut state deficits to help France align itself for a single European currency.

Official figures say the number of unemployed is 3.1 million but many specialists say the real figure is around four million when taking into account many youths on job-training schemes and other flimsy, short-term contracts.

"Jospin can make all the political reforms which he wants to make but it's on employment that he will be judged. If he's doesn't succeed, he'll collapse (in the eyes of the public) like Chirac did," July told French television.
